title: Encryption and Cryptography
summary: From ancient ciphers to the padlock in your browser: how encryption keeps secrets, how codes are broken, how strangers share keys safely, how passwords are stored, and why quantum computers are changing the rules.
learn: How substitution ciphers work and how frequency analysis breaks them
Why keys and key length decide how strong encryption is
How public-key cryptography solves the key-sharing problem
What HTTPS does to protect you on the web
How hashing protects passwords and how end-to-end encryption works
Why quantum computers threaten today's encryption, and the debate about encryption and privacy
intro: Every message you send, every card payment and every website login relies on cryptography. In this topic you'll crack ciphers by hand, discover why key length matters, find out how two strangers can share a secret in public, see what really happens when you visit an HTTPS website, and learn why the world is racing to make encryption "quantum-safe".

pages.spec: Encrypt and decrypt with substitution ciphers and break them using frequency analysis
pages.summary: A substitution cipher swaps each letter for another. It looks secure, but in any language some letters are far more common than others, so counting letter frequencies reveals the pattern and breaks the code.

b: Cryptography: the science of keeping information secret
Plaintext: the readable message
Ciphertext: the scrambled message
Key: the secret that locks and unlocks it
slides.n: Starter answer: CODE BREAKER. Only 25 possible shifts, so you can try them all.

Used for centuries by spies and royalty
So how could anyone break it?

blocks.text: The language of cryptography

**[[cryptography]]** is the science of keeping information secret. Encryption turns readable **[[plaintext]]** into scrambled **[[ciphertext]]** using a **[[key]]**. Decryption uses the key to turn it back. In the Cyber Security topic you met the **Caesar cipher**, which shifts every letter the same number of places. With only 25 possible shifts, it can be cracked in minutes by trying them all.
Substitution ciphers
A **substitution cipher** replaces each letter with any other letter, following a secret alphabet:
There are about 400 million million million million possible keys, far too many to try one by one. For centuries, people thought these ciphers were unbreakable.
Frequency analysis

**[[frequency analysis]]** breaks substitution ciphers by counting how often each letter appears. In English, **E** is the most common letter (about 13% of letters), followed by **T** and **A**. So the most common letter in a long ciphertext probably stands for E. Codebreakers then use word patterns: a one-letter word is probably A or I, and a common three-letter word is probably THE.
Frequency analysis was first described by Al-Kindi, a scholar in Baghdad, in the 800s. It was used to uncover the secret plot that led to the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots in 1587.

blocks.title: Crack the spy message
steps: Your teacher gives you a 200-letter message encrypted with a substitution cipher and an English letter-frequency chart.
Count how many times each letter appears in the ciphertext and record the top five.
Match the most common letters to E, T and A. Fill them in and look for word patterns.
Keep going until you can read the message.

q.q: Which three ciphertext letters were most common, and what did they stand for?
q.a: Depends on the message; usually the most common is E, then T and A (though short messages vary).

q.q: Explain why frequency analysis works on substitution ciphers.
q.a: Each plaintext letter always becomes the same ciphertext letter, so the letter frequencies of the language are kept; the most common ciphertext letters match the most common English letters.

check.q: What is ciphertext?
What is the key in cryptography?
o: The secret used to encrypt and decrypt

check.q: Which is the most common letter in English?
check.why: E makes up about 13% of letters.

check.q: Why is a Caesar cipher easy to break?
o: There are only 25 possible shifts to try

practice.q: Explain the difference between plaintext and ciphertext.
practice.a: Plaintext is the readable/original message (1); ciphertext is the scrambled/encrypted version (1).

practice.q: Describe how frequency analysis can be used to break a substitution cipher.
practice.a: Count how often each letter appears in the ciphertext (1); match the most frequent to the most common English letters such as E, T, A (1); use word patterns/trial and improvement to work out the rest (1).

pages.title: Keys and brute force
pages.spec: Explain why key length matters and describe symmetric encryption
pages.summary: Modern encryption uses mathematics and very long binary keys. A brute-force attack tries every possible key, so each extra bit doubles the work. Symmetric encryption, such as AES, uses the same key to lock and unlock.
pages.starter: A bike lock has 3 dials of 0-9. How many combinations? What if it had 4 dials?
sc: I can explain a brute-force attack
I can explain why longer keys are stronger

b: A brute-force attack tries every possible key until one works
3-dial lock: 1,000 combinations; 4 dials: 10,000
Computers can try billions of keys a second
Defence: make the number of keys astronomically large
Keys are binary numbers: each bit is 0 or 1
8-bit key: 256 possible keys; 128-bit key: about 3.4 × 10³⁸
Each extra bit doubles the number of keys
Brute-forcing a 128-bit key would take longer than the age of the universe
The same key encrypts and decrypts
Fast, so it's used for most data: Wi-Fi, files, video calls
AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is the world standard
Problem: how do you share the key safely?

blocks.text: Brute-force attacks

A **[[brute-force attack]]** tries every possible key until one works. It always succeeds in the end, so the only defence is to make the number of possible keys so large that trying them all would take impossibly long.
Key length
Modern keys are binary numbers. **[[key length]]** is the number of bits in the key. Every extra bit **doubles** the number of possible keys.

blocks.caption: Key length and number of keys
head: Key length
Number of possible keys
Time to try them all at 1 billion keys a second
rows: Trillions of times the age of the universe

blocks.title: Doubling with each bit
blocks.context: How many keys does a 10-bit key have?
steps: Each bit can be 0 or 1, so 2 choices per bit.
blocks.answer: A 10-bit key has 1,024 possible keys. An 11-bit key would have 2,048.

blocks.text: Symmetric encryption

In **[[symmetric encryption]]**, the **same key** encrypts and decrypts, like a front door key that locks and unlocks. It's very fast, so it protects most data: Wi-Fi traffic, files on your phone and video calls. The world standard is **[[AES]]** (Advanced Encryption Standard), with keys of 128 or 256 bits.
Symmetric encryption has a big problem: both people need the same secret key. If you send the key over the internet, anyone listening could copy it. Lesson 3 solves this.

blocks.title: Brute-force race
steps: Partner A sets a secret 2-digit code (00-99); Partner B tries codes one at a time and counts the guesses. Swap.
Now try a 3-digit code. How long do you think it would take?
Use the calculator to work out how long a computer trying 1 billion keys per second would take to try every 56-bit and every 128-bit key.

q.q: How many guesses did it take for 2 digits? How many possible codes were there for 3 digits?
q.a: 2 digits: up to 100 possible codes (on average about 50 guesses); 3 digits: 1,000 possible codes.

q.q: Explain why adding bits to a key makes it so much stronger.
q.a: Each extra bit doubles the number of possible keys, so the time for a brute-force attack doubles each time; long keys make it take longer than the age of the universe.

check.q: What is a brute-force attack?
o: Trying every possible key until one works

check.q: How many keys does a 4-bit key have?
What happens to the number of possible keys when you add one bit?
What is symmetric encryption?
o: Using the same key to encrypt and decrypt

practice.q: Explain why a 128-bit key is much more secure than a 40-bit key.
practice.a: It has far more possible keys (2¹²⁸ vs 2⁴⁰) (1), so a brute-force attack would take impossibly long (1).

practice.q: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of symmetric encryption.
practice.a: Advantage: fast/efficient for lots of data (1); disadvantage: both people need the same key, which is hard to share safely (1).

pages.title: Sharing secrets with strangers
pages.spec: Explain how public-key cryptography lets people communicate securely without first sharing a secret key
pages.summary: Public-key (asymmetric) cryptography uses a pair of keys: a public key anyone can use to lock a message and a private key only the owner can use to unlock it. It is based on maths problems that are easy one way and very hard to reverse.
pages.starter: You want to send a locked box to someone you've never met, but you can't send the key in the post. How could you do it?
sc: I can explain the key-sharing problem
I can describe how public and private keys work
I can explain the idea of a one-way function

b: You send me an open padlock (your public key) and keep its key (your private key)
I put my message in a box and snap your padlock shut
Anyone can see the padlock, but only you can open it
No secret ever had to travel through the post
Public key: shared with everyone, used to encrypt messages to you
Private key: kept secret, used to decrypt them
The two keys are mathematically linked
Also called asymmetric encryption

slides.t: Easy one way, hard to reverse
b: Multiplying two big prime numbers is easy
Finding which two primes made a huge number is incredibly hard
RSA encryption relies on this one-way problem
13 × 17 = 221 is easy; what two primes make 6,557?
slides.n: 6,557 = 79 × 83. Let pupils try with calculators: much harder than multiplying.

blocks.text: The key-sharing problem

Symmetric encryption is fast, but both people need the same secret key. How do you share it with a website you've never visited before, when criminals might be watching everything you send? For thousands of years there was no good answer. Then, in the 1970s, cryptographers (including researchers at GCHQ in the UK, whose work was kept secret for years) found a brilliant solution.
Public-key cryptography
**[[public-key cryptography]]** (also called asymmetric encryption) uses **two** linked keys:
A message encrypted with someone's public key can **only** be decrypted with their private key. So anyone can send them a secret message, but only they can read it.
One-way functions

Public-key cryptography is built on **[[one-way function|one-way functions]]**: maths that is easy to do but extremely hard to reverse. The famous **RSA** system uses prime numbers. Multiplying two large primes is quick, but working out which two primes were multiplied together to make a number hundreds of digits long would take today's computers longer than the age of the universe.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The key-sharing problem: how to agree a secret over a public network
Public key encrypts; private key decrypts
Security relies on maths problems that are very hard to reverse

blocks.title: The padlock post office
steps: Act it out: Alice, Bob and Eve (the eavesdropper). Your teacher gives you a box, padlocks and keys (or paper versions).
Alice must send Bob a secret note. Eve sees everything that passes between them. Use only padlocks: no keys may be sent!
Then try the "double padlock" method: Alice locks, Bob adds his lock, Alice removes hers, Bob removes his.
Record each step and check Eve never had a chance to open the box.

q.q: Describe how Alice sent the secret without ever sending a key.
q.a: Bob sent Alice his open padlock (public key) and kept his key (private key); Alice locked the box with Bob's padlock and sent it; only Bob's private key could open it, so Eve couldn't read it.

q.q: How does this model public-key cryptography?
q.a: The open padlock is the public key that anyone can use to lock (encrypt); the key Bob keeps is the private key that is never shared and is the only way to unlock (decrypt).

check.q: What problem does public-key cryptography solve?
o: Sharing a key safely with someone you've never met

check.q: Which key do you share with everyone?
check.why: Public keys are meant to be shared.

check.q: A message encrypted with Ben's public key can be decrypted by...
Why is RSA hard to break?
o: Finding the two large primes that make a huge number is extremely hard
check.why: It relies on factoring being hard.

practice.q: Explain how public and private keys are used to send a secret message to Sam.
practice.a: The sender gets Sam's public key (1) and uses it to encrypt the message (1); only Sam's private key can decrypt it, and Sam never shares it (1).

practice.q: Explain what is meant by a one-way function, using an example.
practice.a: Something easy to calculate but very hard to reverse (1), e.g. multiplying two large primes is easy, but finding them from the result is very hard (1).

pages.title: The padlock in your browser
pages.spec: Describe how HTTPS uses encryption and certificates to protect communication on the web
pages.summary: HTTPS protects web traffic using TLS. Your browser checks the website's digital certificate to confirm who it is, uses public-key cryptography to agree a secret session key, then encrypts everything with fast symmetric encryption.
pages.starter: You're on public Wi-Fi in a café. Who could see the websites you visit and what you type?
sc: I can explain what HTTPS protects against
I can describe what a digital certificate does
I can outline the steps of an HTTPS connection

b: HTTP sends web pages as plain text: anyone on the network could read them
HTTPS = HTTP Secure: everything is encrypted
Protects passwords, card numbers and messages from eavesdroppers
Look for https:// and the padlock (or settings icon) in the address bar
A digital certificate proves a website is who it says it is
Issued by a trusted certificate authority (CA)
Your browser checks it automatically
Warning screens mean something is wrong: don't continue
1 Browser says hello; website sends its certificate and public key
2 Browser checks the certificate
3 They use public-key cryptography to agree a secret session key
4 Everything after that is encrypted with fast symmetric encryption (like AES)
slides.n: This combines lessons 2 and 3: public-key crypto solves the key-sharing problem, then symmetric crypto does the heavy lifting.

blocks.text: HTTP and HTTPS

Web pages travel across many networks to reach you. With old **HTTP**, the data travelled as plain text, so anyone on the same Wi-Fi, or anywhere along the route, could read it. **[[HTTPS]]** (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) encrypts everything between your browser and the website using a protocol called **[[TLS]]** (Transport Layer Security).
Digital certificates

Encryption is useless if you're securely talking to a fake website. A **[[digital certificate]]** proves a website's identity. It's issued by a trusted **certificate authority**, which checks that the website's owner really controls that domain. Your browser checks certificates automatically and shows a big warning if something is wrong.
The padlock only means your connection is encrypted and the certificate matches the address. It does NOT mean the website is honest: scam sites can have HTTPS too. Always check the address carefully.
The TLS handshake

items: Your browser says hello and lists the encryption methods it supports.
The website replies with its certificate, which includes its public key.
Your browser checks the certificate is valid and was issued for that website.
Using public-key cryptography, they agree a brand-new secret **[[session key]]** that no eavesdropper can learn.
Everything after that is encrypted with fast symmetric encryption (usually AES) using the session key.

blocks.title: Why use both kinds of encryption?
items: Public-key cryptography solves the key-sharing problem, but is slow
Symmetric encryption is fast, but needs a shared key
HTTPS uses public-key crypto to share a session key, then symmetric crypto for the data

blocks.title: Handshake role play
steps: Take the roles of Browser, Website and Eavesdropper. Use the role cards your teacher gives you.
Act out the five handshake steps, passing "messages" on cards. The Eavesdropper copies every card they see.
At the end, check: what did the Eavesdropper learn? Could they read the final message?

q.q: List what the Eavesdropper saw and explain why they still couldn't read the message.
q.a: They saw the hello messages, the certificate and the public key, but not the session key (it was protected by public-key crypto) or the private key, so the encrypted messages were unreadable.

q.q: A browser shows "Your connection is not private". What should you do and why?
q.a: Don't continue: the certificate check failed, so the site may be fake or someone may be intercepting the connection; go back or check the address.

check.q: What does HTTPS do?
o: Encrypts data between your browser and a website

check.q: What does a digital certificate prove?
o: That a site has no adverts
That a website is who it claims to be

check.q: Does a padlock in the address bar mean a website is safe to trust?
o: No: it means the connection is encrypted, but scam sites can have HTTPS too
check.why: Encryption isn't the same as honesty.

check.q: Why does HTTPS use symmetric encryption for the main data?

practice.q: Explain why logging in to a website over HTTP on public Wi-Fi is risky.
practice.a: Data is sent unencrypted/as plain text (1), so someone on the network could read the password (1).

practice.q: Describe how HTTPS uses both public-key and symmetric encryption.
practice.a: Public-key crypto (with the site's certificate/public key) is used to agree/exchange a session key securely (1); the session key is then used with fast symmetric encryption (1) for all the data sent (1).

pages.title: Hashes and private chats
pages.spec: Explain how hashing protects stored passwords and how end-to-end encryption protects messages
pages.summary: Websites shouldn't store your actual password. They store a hash: a fixed-length fingerprint that can't be reversed, often with a random salt. End-to-end encryption means only the people in a conversation can read messages, not even the app company.
pages.starter: If a website emails you your old password when you click "forgot password", what does that tell you about how it stores passwords?
sc: I can explain what a hash function does
I can explain why passwords are hashed and salted

b: A hash function turns any input into a fixed-length "fingerprint"
Same input = same hash; tiny change = totally different hash
One-way: you can't turn a hash back into the input
Used for passwords, checking downloads and digital signatures
Good websites store the hash, not your password
When you log in, they hash what you type and compare
A salt (random extra data) is added so identical passwords get different hashes
If a site can email you your password, it isn't storing it safely
slides.n: Starter answer: it stores passwords in a way that can be read, which is bad practice.

b: Messages are encrypted on the sender's phone and only decrypted on the receiver's
The app company's servers only see ciphertext
Used by WhatsApp, Signal and iMessage
Protects against hackers and snooping, even if the company is hacked

blocks.text: Hash functions
A **[[hash]]** function takes any input (a word, a password, a whole film) and produces a fixed-length string called a hash, like a fingerprint for data.

blocks.caption: Properties of a good hash function
head: Property
What it means
rows: Every hash is the same length, however big the input
The same input always gives the same hash
Changing one letter completely changes the hash
You can't work out the input from the hash

blocks.text: Storing passwords

A well-built website never stores your actual password. It stores the **hash** of your password. When you log in, it hashes what you type and checks whether the two hashes match. If criminals steal the database, they get hashes, not passwords.

To make hashes even safer, websites add a **[[salt]]**: a random string added to each password before hashing. That way, two people with the same password get completely different hashes, and attackers can't use pre-computed tables of common password hashes.
Hashing doesn't protect weak passwords completely. Attackers can hash millions of common passwords to see which match. A long, unique password (like three random words) is still essential.
End-to-end encryption

With **[[end-to-end encryption]]** (E2EE), a message is encrypted on the sender's device and can only be decrypted on the receiver's device. The company running the app passes on scrambled ciphertext and cannot read it. Apps such as Signal, WhatsApp and iMessage use E2EE for messages.

blocks.title: Hash detective
steps: Use the online hash tool your teacher shows (or the printed table of hashes).
Hash the word "password", then "Password", then "password1". Compare the hashes.
Your teacher gives you a "stolen" list of unsalted hashes. Use the table of common password hashes to find which accounts used weak passwords.
Explain how salting would have protected them.

q.q: What happened to the hash when you changed just one letter?
q.a: It changed completely, with no similarity to the original: the avalanche effect.

q.q: Explain how a salt would stop the attack you just did.
q.a: Each password would have a different random salt added before hashing, so the hashes wouldn't match the pre-computed table of common passwords; the attacker would have to start from scratch for every account.

check.q: What does a hash function produce?
o: An encrypted file with a key
A fixed-length fingerprint of the input

check.q: Why do websites store password hashes instead of passwords?
o: If stolen, hashes can't simply be turned back into passwords

check.q: What is a salt?
o: Random data added to a password before hashing
check.why: Salts make identical passwords hash differently.

check.q: With end-to-end encryption, who can read your messages?
o: Only the sender and the receiver
check.why: Only the ends of the conversation.

practice.q: Explain how a website checks your password without storing it.
practice.a: It hashes the password you type (1) and compares it with the stored hash; if they match, you're let in (1).

practice.q: Explain one benefit of end-to-end encryption.
practice.a: Only sender and receiver can read messages (1), so even if the company's servers are hacked/someone intercepts them, messages stay private (1).

pages.title: Quantum threats and the encryption debate
pages.spec: Explain why quantum computers threaten today's public-key encryption and discuss the debate about encryption, privacy and security
pages.summary: Powerful future quantum computers could break RSA and similar public-key systems, so the world is moving to new post-quantum cryptography. Meanwhile, governments and tech companies argue about whether police should be able to access encrypted messages.
pages.starter: Criminals copy encrypted messages today but can't read them. Why might they still want to keep them for 15 years?
sc: I can explain the quantum threat to public-key encryption
I can argue both sides of the encryption backdoor debate

b: A large quantum computer could factor huge numbers quickly using Shor's algorithm
That would break RSA and much of today's public-key encryption
Today's quantum computers are far too small, but they are improving
"Harvest now, decrypt later": attackers store encrypted data to read in future
slides.n: Starter answer: harvest now, decrypt later. Link to the Quantum Computing topic.

b: New encryption based on maths problems quantum computers can't easily solve
In 2024 the US standards body NIST published the first post-quantum standards
Governments, banks and tech companies are already switching
Symmetric encryption like AES-256 is still considered strong
A backdoor: a secret way for authorities to read encrypted messages
For: helps police catch criminals and protect children
Against: a backdoor for the police is a weakness criminals could also use
Should end-to-end encryption have exceptions? People strongly disagree

blocks.text: The quantum threat

A **[[quantum computer]]** uses the strange rules of quantum physics to solve some problems far faster than ordinary computers. In 1994 the mathematician Peter Shor showed that a large enough quantum computer could find the prime factors of huge numbers quickly, which would break RSA and other public-key systems that protect HTTPS, banking and messaging.

Today's quantum computers are far too small and error-prone to do this, but they're improving. Attackers may already be using **"harvest now, decrypt later"**: copying encrypted data today to read when quantum computers are ready. That's a problem for secrets that must stay secret for decades, like medical records or state secrets.
Post-quantum cryptography

**[[post-quantum cryptography]]** is new encryption based on maths problems that are hard even for quantum computers. In 2024 the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) published the first post-quantum encryption standards, and the UK's National Cyber Security Centre has set out a timeline for organisations to migrate over the next decade. Some messaging apps and browsers already use post-quantum methods alongside the old ones.
Symmetric encryption like AES is much less affected: quantum computers would roughly halve its effective strength, so using 256-bit keys keeps it safe.
The encryption debate

Strong encryption protects everyone's privacy, but it also hides criminals' messages. Some governments want a **[[backdoor]]**: a special way for authorities to read encrypted messages when they have a legal warrant.

Against
